summary: This program declares two boolean variables, prints their values, and then combines them with logical operators to work out a third value. It shows that a boolean can only ever hold true or false, and that Java can calculate one boolean from others.

lines.text: A boolean variable stores one of exactly two values, true or false. Notice that true is a Java keyword, not the text "true" in quotes, so no quotation marks belong here.
When a boolean is joined to a string with +, Java converts it to the word true or false for display, which is why the output reads as plain English.

This is the logical part: ! flips hasBugs from false to true, and && demands that both sides be true before the whole expression is true. The value is computed from the other two variables rather than typed in by hand.
The result is true here because Java is fun and there are no bugs; change either starting variable and this line reports a different answer, which is the decision tree in action.
